title: Protein atlas
summary: From Cells' own law inventory, with links out to the public protein atlases.
caveat: Shapes are schematic, drawn from subunit counts, and not to scale. A grey form is a generic law: no protein is assigned.

plan.where: What the engine models today (stage 2 inventory)

gained_review.text: Reviews on 14 and 15 November 2026 found no channel, pump, transporter or junction law among them. Two cases are the lead's to classify: secretion and uptake across a membrane, and the binding of molecules to sites.

mappings.label: Assigned in source
mappings.description: The law, its documents or the source it cites names the protein. This records a label; the kind of evidence on each law says what stands behind it.

mappings.label: Candidate
mappings.description: The law models a named native current or channel class. Which gene products carry it is the inventory's inference.
mappings.note: Which protein carries this current is the inventory's inference. The shape drawn is the candidate's.

mappings.label: Generic
mappings.description: The law is deliberately generic, phenomenological or manufactured. Products are listed as candidates only.
mappings.note: The law is generic: it names no protein. The grey form is a plain stand-in, and any products below are candidates only.

evidence.label: Expressed isoform
evidence.description: The cited data come from the named isoform, expressed on its own.

evidence.label: Isoform named in the title
evidence.description: The cited source names the isoform in its title; the inventory read no further detail.

evidence.label: Native current
evidence.description: The cited data are a current recorded from native cells, not from an isolated isoform.

evidence.label: Neuron model
evidence.description: The cited source is a model of a neuron.

evidence.label: Derived reduction
evidence.description: A reduced (Morris-Lecar) form of the named channel.

evidence.label: Designed protein
evidence.description: An engineered protein with no natural gene product.

evidence.label: No detail in the source
evidence.description: The source gives no detail on what the coefficients were measured from.

site_note: Where the engine's law acts, read from the law's name and documents.

reference.label: Human
reference.plain: The inventory names its candidate gene products by their human genes. Every other species is read against them.
method: Each unit's candidate gene products are the law inventory's own.
Accessions, protein names and lengths are from reviewed human UniProt entries.
Where the inventory found a Xenopus laevis entry for the same gene, the product links to it. Those entries are links only, not products of their own.

findings.sentence: This species builds the machine from another protein family.

findings.sentence: The search found no gene product for this unit.

species.no_entry: This atlas has no entry for this unit.

found_by.label: Family signature
found_by.description: Its own record carries the signature of a family that makes the machine. A candidate by family, not an established counterpart.
found_by.line: Candidate by family, not an established counterpart
found_by.extra_description: Its own record carries the signature of the family named. It matches no unit of the inventory, so it is a candidate for none.

found_by.label: Accessory family
found_by.description: Its own record carries only the signature of a family that goes with the machine: a regulator, or a subunit that makes no channel or pump by itself. Listed with the machine; no candidate for the machine's own work.
found_by.line: Goes with the machine, no candidate for its own work
found_by.extra_description: Its own record carries only the signature of a family that goes with a machine of the inventory, a machine no protein of this species makes. It is a candidate for no unit.

found_by.label: Named in a publication
found_by.description: A paper names this gene or protein in this species.

found_by.label: Similarity search
found_by.description: Found by sequence similarity to a named protein of another species. A candidate, not an established counterpart.
found_by.line: Candidate by similarity, not an established counterpart
found_by.extra_description: Found by sequence similarity to a named protein of another species. It matches no unit of the inventory, so it is a candidate for none.

found_by.label: Not stated
found_by.description: An older file does not say how this product was found.

entry_kinds.label: Reviewed entry
entry_kinds.description: A UniProtKB entry that a curator reviewed. That says how the entry was written, not what the protein does in this species.
entry_kinds.line: Its UniProtKB entry was reviewed by a curator. That says how the entry was written, not what the protein does in this species.

entry_kinds.label: Unreviewed entry
entry_kinds.description: A UniProtKB entry annotated automatically, by rule systems and prediction programs.
entry_kinds.line: Its UniProtKB entry was annotated automatically, by rule systems and prediction programs.

entry_kinds.label: Genome annotation
entry_kinds.description: A gene model, or a protein of a genome record, annotated by its submitters, with no UniProtKB entry of its own.
entry_kinds.line: It is a gene model, or a protein of a genome record, with no UniProtKB entry of its own.

entry_kinds.label: Not stated
entry_kinds.description: An older file does not say what this product's record is.
entry_kinds.line: Its file does not say what its record is.

shelves.note: Where a protein or a family of a species' own catalogue is looked up. A species is named by its id; a pattern with a kind applies to the proteins whose mark 'kind' has that value; 'family' is for a family or a group that is an InterPro entry. Each pattern says when it was checked and what answered.

shelves.limits_note: A species' shelves.json stays under 1 MB, and so does each file of its families' members (schema/SPECIES_PROTEINS.md, Size). A species named here has bounds of its own, in bytes, each with since when and why; every other species keeps the shared ones.

xenopus.why: The frog's catalogue is the largest of all, with both copies of a gene shown: its shelves are over 1 MB. Its members are cut 6,000 to a file where the others' are cut 2,000, so that its catalogue adds 6 files of members to the page and not 18 (the page holds at most 511 files), and each such file is over 1 MB. Decided on 19 November 2026, when the frog was added.

voltage-gated Na channel.plain: A sodium channel that opens when the membrane voltage rises. One long protein chain folds into four repeats around a single pore, and smaller beta subunits sit beside it.

voltage-gated K channel.plain: A potassium channel that opens with the membrane voltage. Four subunits surround one pore.
voltage-gated K channel.plain_generic: A voltage-gated potassium current in a simple phenomenological form.

inward-rectifier K channel.plain: A potassium channel that conducts best near the resting voltage and helps to hold the cell there. Four subunits surround one pore.

Ca-activated K channel.plain: A potassium channel opened by calcium inside the cell.

HCN channel.plain: A channel that opens when the membrane voltage falls, and passes both potassium and sodium. Four subunits surround one pore.

background leak.plain: An always-open path for ions through the membrane: a background conductance.

background permeability.plain: A property of the membrane as a whole: how easily ions or water cross it. No protein population stands behind it.

voltage-gated Ca channel (HVA).plain: A calcium channel that opens at high voltage. One long chain folds into four repeats around the pore, with a beta subunit inside the cell and an alpha2-delta subunit outside.

voltage-gated Ca channel (LVA).plain: A calcium channel that opens at low voltage (T-type). One long chain forms the pore on its own.

gap-junction channel.plain: A channel that joins two neighbouring cells, so ions and small molecules pass straight from one to the other. Each cell contributes a ring of six connexins.
gap-junction channel.plain_generic: A channel that joins two neighbouring cells, so ions and small molecules pass straight from one to the other.

P-type ATPase.plain: A pump: it spends ATP to move ions against their gradient.

secondary transporter.plain: An exchanger: it moves one ion uphill by letting another run downhill.

secondary transporter (SLC12).plain: A cotransporter: it carries chloride together with potassium, or with sodium and potassium, and moves no net charge.

configured transporter.plain: A transporter that each model configuration declares: its stoichiometry and identity come from the configuration.

intracellular release channel.plain: A channel in the ER membrane that releases stored calcium into the cell.

organelle permeability.plain: The passive permeability of the mitochondrial inner membrane, lumped into one term.

protein assembly.plain: An engineered protein cage: 60 subunits in 20 three-part units, which assemble into a closed shell.

left_out.reason: it is a designed protein, not a part of a cell
left_out.why: The user, 15 November 2026: protein assemblies are one feature today and out of character with the rest of the picture, whose parts are all real or planned things of a cell; assembly may return later for a real machine, such as a proteasome. While this entry stands, the scene builder does not draw the unit: its district (Protein cage), its site (Cytoplasm) and its kind of evidence (Designed protein) hold nothing else and go with it, the counts on the page are of what is drawn, and the wording below stands in for the text that names a designed protein. The inventory still has the unit, and each species' atlas file keeps its entry for it. Remove this entry and all of that comes back as it was.
